speechtext:
On Saturday last the government
spent a very substantial part of the day in considering the financial position of the four western provinces, especially in view of the representations that recently have been made as to the amount of -money they will require, in excess of what they expect to derive from taxation, to meet what they conceive to be their requirements. A telegraphic communication was sent to the premiers of the four provinces suggesting that their legislatures might adjourn over Easter, in which event

either the premiers or their representatives might meet the government here on Thursday, April 5, for the purpose of discussing the situation.
The government of Manitoba had made arrangements contemplating an early adjournment, and suggested that a later date would best suit their convenience. The province of Saskatchewan, having telephoned Manitoba and Alberta, sent a telegram in much the same sense. Alberta did not reply directly, or in other than the manner I have just indicated, as suggested by the telegram from Saskatchewan. British Columbia suggested that the position of the prairie provinces was somewhat different from their position and that the matters might be discussed at a later date as they were making arrangements for prorogation. Last evening I dispatched a message to the four western provinces indicating that apparently any day next week would not be a satisfactory date on which to discuss the matters, and that they might stand to a date to be mutually agreed upon.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. 42, respecting relief measures.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking any part in this debate until I heard the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) read extracts yesterday from the report of the auditor general and his findings in connection with the expenditure and distribution of federal aid to the different provinces. When I heard those quotations I decided that I should make my voice heard, not to say to the government "I told you so," but to draw attention to the fact that in 1932 I made certain charges in connection with the expenditure of federal aid in certain sections of the province of New Brunswick. At that time I called the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) to the fact that paysheets had been padded by placing upon them the names of men who had not done one day's work. I read six or seven affidavits which I offered to the minister. I demanded that an investigation be held and I put my seat at stake. I stated that if at least ninety per cent of the charges contained in those affidavits and the charges made by myself could not be proved before a proper tribunal, I would resign my seat in parliament. I offered these affidavits to the Minister of Labour but he refused to accept them. He told me, as he has often told the house since, that the matter rested entirely with the provincial authorities of New Brunswick and that his department could have nothing to do with an investigation. I refused to allow these charges to be investigated by the provincial authorities but I was prepared to have them investigated by a properly constituted tribunal to be named by the government or by the house.
In the quotations from the report of the auditor general, that official states that in New Brunswick as well as elsewhere he found padded paysheets and that the federal government had paid its share of amounts which it had no right to pay under the law. He stated also that paysheets and accounts were not properly kept, so I decided it was my duty to direct the attention of the house to the warning I gave the government in 1932. On that occasion I spoke from personal knowledge of the way in which things had been carried
Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Veniot

on in certain sections of New Brunswick. I was told by some hon. members opposite that I was decrying my own province, running down my own people. No; it was not my intention to decry my province but to point out to the government of this dominion the necessity for better regulations, a stricter inspection of the way in which the work was being carried on under the relief measure, and if possible putting a stop to this graft and maladministration in connection with federal aid not only in the province of New Brunswick but elsewhere-because I see from the auditor general's report that the same condition of affairs exists, in connection with the -distribution of expenditures of federal money for unemployment purposes, all over the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Are these the same charges which the hon. member preferred in 1932?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I do not know whether the auditor general refers to them or not, but I am now referring to the 1932 charges.

speechtext: Was not an investigation being held by the provincial government of New Brunswick at the time the hon. member made that statement in the house in 1932?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Not of the accounts in
reference to which I read affidavits in this house. An investigation was being held into expenditures of road money in the county of Westmorland; I am not referring to that investigation nor to the charges made and investigated at that time. In 1932 the affidavits I read referred to bridge work in Restigouche county, expenditures in connection with which were not being investigated, and I also referred to road work in the county of -Gloucester which has never been investigated. The auditor general's report now bears me out. It shows that I was right when I warned the government against the way things were being done, and advised that measures, stricter than those already in force, should be taken to prevent this maldistribution of public funds of the dominion. I was perfectly right. The auditor general now points out, as I have stated before, that not only in the distribution of direct relief but in the distribution of aid to unemployment in the matter of public works, fraud has existed, accounts have not been properly kept and paysheets have been padded.
The auditor general, or the person whom he sent to investigate these accounts in the various provinces, had only a slim chance to go into these matters. But slim as was that
[Mr- Veniot.]
chance, we find that the condition has been rampan-t throughout every province in the dominion. In 1930, when the first $20,000,000 was voted for aid to unemployment, the official opposition warned the government against the methods they were adopting to have the money expended. We claimed that there were not sufficient safeguards surrounding the expenditure of the money, and we asked that an audit be made on the part of the dominion. But our friends opposite pooh-poohed the idea; they told us that it would be insulting the provinces and the municipalities if we insisted on an audit. Well, to-day they are insisting on an audit, but they have locked the barn door after the horse has been stolen. It will be impossible to have an adequate audit of the operations of the last four years, but I do hope that a very strict audit, in accordance with the order in council of March 10 last, will be made in the future. But when you have the proof from our own auditor general that crooked work has 'been carried on in these expenditures is it possible that the present government is going to entrust to the same individuals, who were guilty of this crooked work, the expenditure of money for unemployment relief, either directly or indirectly, according to the terms of the bill now before the house? I say that those in authority who permitted this maladministration are not fit to continue the administration of any money which this parliament might vote for unemployment relief either directly or indirectly, and that another system should be adopted by which the dominion could more properly safeguard its interests.
Last evening my colleague, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud), referred to certain projects in 1933 that had been carried on in the province of New Brunswick. He said, and rightly so, that the money in connection with these projects had all been expended weeks and months before the projects were approved by the federal Department of Labour. That approval was given on October 10, I believe, whereas the money in connection with these projects had been all expended in August and September, and perhaps in July. Let me say to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska that that has not been uncommon since the inauguration of this relief system, because in 1931, hundreds of thousands of dollars were expended in New Brunswick before a single project had been approved. The projects of 1931 were approved on November 26, and in July, August and September, and part of October, all this money

*Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Veniot
had been expended. There had been no inspection whatever of the projects submitted to the government for unemployment relief in the matter of public works in that province, and I condemned that transaction at the time. I called the attention of the minister at the time to this fact and insisted that in the future no projects should be accepted by the Department of Labour unless they were first examined by an engineer representing the federal government and approved and recommended by him. But evidently that was a suggestion that has not been carried out, at least in the province of New Brunswick.
Now there is a bill before the legislature of New Brunswick authorizing the government of that province to expend $10,000,000 on hard-surface roads. Let me say to the Minister of Labour that the province of New Brunswick cannot afford under present conditions to spend any such amount of money on roads. New Brunswick, with a debt today of approximately $68,000,000, cannot afford to increase that debt by from $10,000,000 to $20,000,000, as the case may be, under present conditions. The government have stated in this house on different occasions that restraint should be placed upon the expenditures of provincial governments, that these governments have been extravagant, and are constantly coming to the Dominion government seeking financial aid. If ever there was an occasion when the government of Canada should restrict any expenditure which is unnecessary it is in the case of the province of New Brunswick. I may be told that this government have no authority over the expenditures of that province. I well know that, but this government have control over the amount of money they will expend in furthering hard surfaced road projects in that province. In that way and to that extent this government can regulate an expenditure which I claim is not necessary at the present time and which the province of New Brunswick cannot afford.
I may be told that this work is required to help unemployment. I am in favour of helping to relieve unemployment. I am prepared to support any measure within reason to help the unemployed in my native province. But there are other means by which the unemployed can be helped, with more permanent effect than by the expenditure on the part of the dominion government of six or seven million dollars for hard surfaced roads in that province. Here let me point out to the Minister of Labour that in the province of New Brunswick there are not more than two
or three municipalities-I doubt if there are three-that are able to take advantage of the government's back to the land policy by paying their $200 share for each settler. Our municipalities are almost bankrupt. They have been brought to that position through the enormous sums that they have had to pay to relieve unemployment, especially by the method of direct relief. The municipalities of New Brunswick cannot take advantage of the Gordon back to the land scheme-I think that is the name by which it is known to-day. Let the government, instead of contributing large sums towards the construction of permanent roads, contribute a larger amount as their share to encourage this back to the land project. At present under that act the federal government pays, I understand, S200 per settler, the province pays $200, and the municipality $200. The municipalities cannot meet that demand. 'Let the provincial government pay its $200 and let the federal Department of Labour add another $200 to what they have already offered, using that money to place unemployed men on new farms in the province of New Brunswick; in that way they will be doing something to establish these people permanently so that in future depressions they will not need to call upon the country to help them. Let me say that the employment afforded by a system of permanent hard surfaced road construction in New Brunswick will not be commensurate with the amount of money expended. We know this work will be done by contract, that the contractor will employ machinery as much as possible and as little hand labour as he can get away with. Therefore the unemployed will not benefit nearly as much as if they were helped to establish themselves permanently on farms. I think I am correct in saying that the auditor general stated that he found in many cases the provinces charging rental to the dominion government for machinery belonging to the province. While he did not condemn such a charge he did state that in many cases the rental was exorbitant. In commenting on that statement I do not wish to reflect at all upon the Minister of Labour, but I am informed that the Minister of Labour himself is perhaps to blame for permitting rental to be charged for the use of provincial machinery on provincial roads. He is also to blame for the exorbitant rental charged, by allowing the ministers of public works of the different provinces to fix what the rental should be, instead of agreeing upon or setting a charge per machine or whatever article is charged for. I have in my hand the report from the

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Veniot

Daily Mail of March 14 last of a speech made in the legislature of New Brunswick. It appears that the leader of the opposition there, Mr. Dysart, attacked the Minister of Public Works for having purchased a machine costing $24,000 and charging it up to federal aid. The Minister of Public Works in defending himself against that charge made the statement that he told the Minister of Labour:
-that it was not practical to use the money received from Ottawa for relief purposes on the trans-Canada highway entirely. . . . The federal Minister of Labour had stated at that time that the provincial government might buy equipment to carry on work and the rental of same could be charged to the dominion government. Consequently, in place of $24,000 being spent as stated by the leader of the opposition, five per cent of the value of the machine was charged as rental and the provincial government absorbed fifty per cent of the cost.
Whether it was fifty per cent of the rental, or of the cost of the machine, that was absorbed is not clearly stated in that speech, but I take it it was fifty per cent of the cost of the machine. If that is so, $12,000 was paid by the federal government, for a machine purchased and owned by the province. No wonder the auditor general says that the rental charged in many cases was exorbitant.
The auditor general also refers to the discovery that ordinary patrol work in the province of New Brunswick was charged up against federal aid, and the federal government called upon to pay its share. I brought that matter up in this house in 1932, I showed where men engaged by the season or by the year on patrol work were included in the items charged against the federal government for unemployment relief. That was not giving relief to the unemployed. These men were paid so much a month, I believe, because their work could be carried on only from May until the end of October or November, according to the season. Those men were regularly employed; what right had they to receive money under unemployment relief? They were receiving regular salaries; that should have been sufficient, and the men without work should have been given a chance to earn the money which was paid these men.
This situation does not exist only in New Brunswick; it is to be found in different sections of Canada. I brought up the matter in this house, but the Minister of Labour would not heed my warning. Now he is brought face to face with the statement made by the auditor general, an official not of the government but of this House of Commons. The minister would not accept the warning as to this kind of expenditure which was given in
{.Mr. Veniot.]
the house, but he is forced to accept the statement made by the auditor general.
The auditor general draws attention to something else which I brought up in the house in 1932, and I think again in 1933. I directed the attention of the minister to the fact that the provincial government had submitted a plan to the minister asking for federal aid in the construction of a power line from Dalhousie to Jacquet River, in which the share of the federal government was to be approximately $27,000. I pointed out to the minister at that time that this enterprise would bring in sufficient revenue to pay for the cost of construction and the upkeep and that the federal government had no right to share the cost of a project under the guise of unemployment relief which could be constructed by the province under the supervision of the hydro commission. In his report the auditor general refers to this matter. He does not condemn it as I condemned it at the time, but no doubt that is because he does not know it is a revenue producing enterprise and that the province of New Brunswick could have constructed that line without incurring one cent of debt that could not be met within a given number of years by means of a proper sinking fund. The report goes on to indicate that even in connection with that enterprise the accounts were not properly kept, and that refunds should be made to the federal government.
I wish now to touch on the question of direct relief. In 1933 I pointed out to the minister that the administration of direct relief was subject to abuse. At the time I referred only to the province of New Brunswick, and I was told by hon. gentlemen opposite that I was decrying my own province. The statement I made then, however, has been endorsed by the auditor general with regard to every province of Canada. I said then, and I will repeat it now-and I have more evidence now than I had then-that there was grave maladministration of direct relief. I showed that men with money in the bank were receiving direct relief. I showed that men who were in receipt of pensions, not as returned soldiers but from other sources, were in receipt of direct relief. I pointed out that men were receiving direct relief who were not entitled to it under the act. To-day we find the auditor general pointing out that in many cases direct relief has been granted to persons who should not be under that scheme. He goes further and points out that in certain parts of New Brunswick where medical aid, dental services and medicine were not provided for, such

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Veniot
accounts were entered as food. That occurred in more than one municipality, and at another point these items were rendered as clothing. Thus the authorities in Ottawa were deceived, because the municipalities knew very well that if the government knew these accounts represented medical attendance, dental services or medicine the government would not pay their share, and rightly so, because that was not the policy. So the statement I made at that time has been substantiated by the report submitted by the auditor general. If that gentleman had time to go further into the matter he would find that in certain sections of New Brunswick municipal councillors rendered accounts to the municipalities for services as councillors in the distribution of relief. Those accounts were paid, and I say that was a direct violation of the municipal act. That practice was followed in the county of Gloucester until this year, when the question was submitted to the attorney general of the province for a legal opinion. He stated that they should not receive remuneration in any case. I know of one councillor who sent in a bill for S166 for visits said to have been made in his parish to see whether certain people required relief.

In conclusion may I crave the indulgence of the house to speak on one other point, because I believe the time at my disposal has almost expired. I believe it was the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) who stated yesterday that there was in existence an organization operating throughout Canada in opposition to the lumber industry. I do not know to what organization he refers, unless he had in mind communistic activities which prevail in the province of Ontario and in the western provinces. Thank God we have very little, if any, communistic activity in New Brunswick. Let me say to some of the lumbermen in eastern Canada, not to all of them but to the great majority, that if they wish their industry to prosper and if they wish to meet the better conditions for the lumber industry appearing on the horizon, they will have to pay their men better wages than they are paying to-day. The trouble with the lumbermen in New Brunswick is that they are not paying wages sufficient to encourage the men to go to and remain in the camps. What do you think, Mr. Speaker, of a lumberman who is paying $10 to $18 a month for the services of a lumberjack? What do you think of a lumber firm which

will send a man into the woods and pay him $1.25 or $1.50 per cord for pulpwood? That man has to cut the pulpwood, load it and pile it. He has to pay from sixty cents to seventy cents per day for board in the camp operated by the lumber company. Under those conditions he cannot make a living. Let me warn the lumbermen of the province of New Brunswick the sooner they recognize that reasonable wages should be paid to the men in the bush the better will they get along in their industry.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why this legislation has been delayed until this late date in the session. Parliament adjourns tomorrow for the Easter recess and does not reassemble until April 9. On the thirty-first of this month the relief bill of 1934 will have expired and unless this legislation is passed before the house adjourns to-morrow, the distribution of relief will automatically cease. Parliament is confronted with the necessity of passing legislation introduced only yesterday and which cannot have due consideration or of assuming the responsibility of depriving pepole of relief without which they cannot get along. Parliament has been in session for many weeks and there has been practically no important legislation before us. This and other bills should have been in our hands a month ago in order that we might give proper consideration to the matters involved. Instead of that, we find legislation being withheld until the very last minute. We are now up against the necessity of either putting this bill through by to-morrow night or assuming the responsibility of depriving people of their relief. I do not know what the government has in view in withholding legislation until the last minute. If their purpose is to get it through without due consideration, then I must congratulate them upon the success of their tactics. Parliament was not created and is not maintained for the purpose of putting through legislation without consideration, it was created for an entirely different purpose, to give consideration to important measures of this kind. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was sitting on this side of the house there was no man in Canada who was more insistent on maintaining the rights of parliament but since he has become Prime Minister he is an entirely different man. We have never had a Prime Minister who was so intent upon usurping the rights of parliament and reducing it to a position of subservience. He is now repeating his performance of last year, of the year before and of the year before that by bringing down legislation at a time when we have to put it through almost without notice and without due consideration or assume the responsibility of depriving people of their relief.
I support my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the statements he made yesterday with regard to auditing the accounts of the provinces in connection with relief expenditures. I remember the fall of 1930 when the leader of the opposition was insistent that an audit of these expenditures sh.ould be carried on continuously. I remember also how the Prime Minister objected
and said that it would be an insult to the provinces to tell them that we were going to audit their accounts. But what happened? We have the report quoted yesterday by the leader of the opposition in which it is stated that the provinces have collected the gasoline tax from their own people and then collected the same tax over again from the federal government. The idea of these measures was to reimburse the provinces for the money they spent, not for the money they collected. The more they collect from the people, the more they collect from us. They have been collecting from us, not on the basis of money spent but on the basis of money collected.
If I understand the bill aright, its aim is to cure unemployment by the launching of an extensive program of public works. Surely the government has learned by this time that unemployment cannot be cured by the construction of public works. Other countries have tried and are trying it and surely the government can learn something from its own experience. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has asked us to give the government credit for being able to make its own mistakes; I wish we could give it credit for being able to profit by them, but I am afraid we cannot.

speechtext: The only way unemployment can be cured in this or any other country is by a revival of industry. Every measure that tends to retard the revival of industry will increase unemployment; every measure that tends to decrease the burden upon industry will tend to cure unemployment. What is the trouble with industry to-day? The trouble is that the costs of conducting industry are greater than the returns to be expected.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, "WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS

I do not care what industry you are engaged in, whether it be farming, lumbering, manufacturing or a commercial enterprise, the expenses to-day in connection with carrying on that industry are greater than the returns you can expect to receive. That is the reason why industry in this country is stagnant and the only remedy is to remove some of the burdens which industry carries upon its shoulders.
One of the greatest burdens of industry is that of taxation. The Associated Chambers

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Young
of Commerce of this country have estimated that one-third of the national income is collected in the form of taxes by the various taxing bodies. If the figures quoted are correct, then the Chambers of Commerce have under-stated the case. If one-third of the national income is collected in taxes, that one-third is part of the national income. That is to say, the national income is the sum of the incomes of all the people. If the wealth created in this country is represented by two, that two represents the incomes of those engaged in industry. If the government collects one unit of that two in the form of taxes and turns it over to another class of people, the amount so collected becomes the income of those people and helps to make up the national income. Therefore, the national income becomes three but the taxes collected are one. That is one-third of the national income but one-half of the created wealth. So that if the figures of the chamber of commerce are correct we are collecting one-half of the created wealth of the country in the form of taxation. That is a burden that industry cannot stand. It means that whether you work at the plough, or at the bench, or at the lathe, or in the counting house, one-half of the product of your labour is being absorbed in the form of taxes. This measure before us, calculated to relieve unemployment by creating public works, will have the effect of increasing the tax burden of the country, and to increase the tax burden is to increase the burden on the back of industry, and therefore create more unemployment rather than reduce it.
Last year the building industry was only 15 per cent of normal. Why was it so low? Why do men not build houses? The first thing a man does when he contemplates putting up a house is to figure what it will cost him, and then he adds what the taxes will be after it is finished, and if the cost of the building, together with the taxes he will have to pay, is greater than the probable value of the building, he will not build. A proposal of this nature, which will add to the cost of building and add to the taxes that will have to be paid on the building afterwards, will further discourage him, so that instead of 15 per cent of normal, building will be less than that. Therefore your public undertakings, public works created to relieve unemployment, will result in more unemployment because it will discourage the building and other industries under private enterprise.
In 1930 we had before the house a bill which proposed to spend S20,000,000 on such [Mr. ymrng.l
a thing as this, to relieve unemployment. At that time we on this side warned the government that it could not be done. We told them that it would not relieve unemployment in the slightest degree; for before you can spend a dollar on public works you must collect that dollar from the people; and when you collect your dollars from the people you reduce their purchasing power by that amount, and when a man's purchasing power is reduced he buys less goods, so that the merchant sells less, the railways haul less, the factories produce less, and there is less employment in the country. So that these schemes which are put forward for curing unemployment through the creation of public works have this effect, that you might create a dollar's worth of employment where you spend a dollar, but you create a dollar's worth of unemployment where you collect the dollar, and the last condition is worse-worse, I say, because in addition to the expenditure on your public works you are saddling yourself with a maintenance cost which will reduce the purchasing power of the people in future years.
I know that some people say that we will print new money to pay for these works; we will not borrow the money but will print it and circulate it. What is the difference? When you print money you really borrow it. When you borrow money in the old fashioned way from the bank, or on debentures or bonds, you borrow from the rich and undertake to pay them back principal with interest; but when you borrow money by printing it you borrow chiefly from poor people and you do not pay them back either principal or interest. That is the essential difference between borrowing in the old fashioned way and printing money. I have here a Canadian dollar bill which states that the dominion will pay to bearer one dollar on demand. It is nothing but a promissory note, and if you print money to pay for these works you will be paying for them with promissory notes. What is the effect? The effect is this, that those who are engaged in productive industry will have to support not only their own industries but other unproductive works which it is proposed, I presume, to create under the provisions of this bill. What kind of works will they be? I do not know, but section 3, subsection (a) says that the governor in council may:
Provide for special relief,

I do not know why the comma is there.
-works and undertakings under control and direction of the Department of National Defence and the Department of the Interior.

Relief Act, 1934

Mr. Young
No limitation is set to the amount of money to be spent, no control over the works to be engaged in. Unlimited sums could be spent and the most fantastic schemes could be engaged in. They could undertake to build a paved highway across Canada, something which would be stupendously expensive to keep up later on. And what good would it be to anyone except a few tourists? Under the provisions of this act they could undertake, at Canadian expense alone, to build the St. Lawrence waterway. Not only that, but having started it, they could carry it on long after the expiration of this act, because section 10 declares:
This act shall expire on the thirty-first day of March, 1935, but any obligation or liability incurred or created under the authority of this act prior to the thirty-first day of March. 1935, together with any liability for expenditures after that date for projects required to be completed in order to preserve the value of work already done may be paid and discharged out of the consolidated revenue fund notwithstanding the expiration of this act on the said date.
That is to say, they can undertake any works, and provided those works are undertaken before the end of March next they can commit this country, they will commit this country, to carry on such works to completion no matter what the expenditure might be. Under this act the Minister of National Defence-because he comes into it-could build fortifications in the arctic circle and no one could stop him.
Have hon. members considered what it would cost to maintain these works? The maintenance cost of public works must be stupendous, and yet it will all be charged against productive industry for all time. And then what will the government do with the unemployed in the remote districts? You cannot put up public buildings in every city, town, village and hamlet in Canada. These works must be located in certain places, and they are bound to be remote from a great many of the unemployed. You cannot take a married man away from home and set him to work in some far distant place without paying him sufficient wages to maintain himself at the works and his family at home, so that you will pay wages out of proportion to the value of the work done.
There are some public works which, perhaps, if the government is bound to adopt a policy such as this, they might consider, namely, public works of the kind which would be at least self-supporting and which would
not saddle us in the future with maintenance costs. For instance, they might turn their attention to reforestation projects. They might reforest some of the waste lands, and in some of the prairie sections, where land is not fit for agriculture, it might be worth while to make experiments in the growing of trees adapted to that country to see whether the monotony of the prairies could be broken and these lands put to some useful purpose.

I am glad to hear it. They might also turn their attention to the draining of some of our lands. I am not an authority on this, but I have been informed that in some of the timbered areas trees would grow more quickly and be bigger if the water table were lowered somewhat. I do not know whether that is correct, but if it is, then a very profitable expenditure could be made in the direction of lowering the water table to promote the growth of timber in such areas. We have in some of our agricultural lands areas that would be better if drained; they would be more easily reclaimed. In some of the drier sections of the prairies it might be profitable, and I believe it is being considered, to find ways and means of catching the spring water and holding it against the drier summer season; not that enough water could be held to affect the climate seriously, but such reservoirs would help in the dry season and would provide men with water for their stock.
I would point out to the government that on the whole the financial situation of the country is such that we cannot afford to indulge in one dollar of unnecessary expenditure. We have to take care of the unemployed; we cannot see people starve in our midst; but the only thing to do is to do it in the cheapest way, and I submit that a program of public works is not the most economical way. We had some experience of it in 1930, when we found that it cost the
Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Pouliot

treasury $4 to put $1 in the hands of a worker. That is to say, for every $4 we spent, $1 went in wages and the other $3 for material and so on. I would suggest to the minister that he should not confine his expenditures to public works but should find cheaper ways of extending relief to people who are in great need.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, in the special session
of 1930 the Prime Minister spoke thus on September 16, as reported at page 238 of Hansard:
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving that you do now leave the chair, I do so because of the disturbed conditions that exist in this country and because of the circumstances that this parliament has been called to consider the problem of unemployment. I indicated a few days ago that the measures proposed were three in number, of which a tariff measure was one. Our tariff measure is not a general revision of the tariff, but deals only with such items in the tariff as it is believed will ensure additional employment to a large number of men and women in Canada.
This was a great speech. A little further on the Prime Minister continued as follows:
It is not for the purposes of protection that the tariff is being revised to-day. The resolutions that are being submitted to this house are not for the purpose of affording protection in the sense in which that term is usually used; but if that term is used to designate just what we, during the election, indicated that it did mean, namely, the giving to Canadians an equality of opportunity with others who are building up their country to enable us to build up our dominion, and to give fair competition to the worker in Canada, be it man or woman, then it is protection that we propose.	There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, in the mind of any lion, gentleman within sound of my voice, that this government at least has a mandate to give effect to that policy.
It was naturally an experiment.
In every part of this dominion I was at great care to make it known to the audiences who listened to what I had to say, so that there could be no mistake as to what I meant, that in the event of their supporting candidates of our party they thereby supported a policy that would ensure fair competition to Canadian workmen and work women and equality of opportunity to Canadians to build up their country.
That sounded very nice. He continued thus:
A number of items only will be dealt with. They will be dealt with on the basis of the employment that will he given to those who are not now employed. And we have very definite assurances from the producers in this country-
Mark that, sir.
-that as a result of the action we are taking they will increase the number of men and

women in their mills and factories. I said the other day, Mr. Speaker, that the number might be estimated at 25,000 within a reasonable time. I think that is too low an estimate, but I desired that the estimate should he at least conservative-as in keeping with the party for which I speak at this moment. When I say 25,000 I think I am understating the number of men and women who will find employment by reason of the action we are taking.
I shall now ask the hon. gentleman in this most important debate to answer from his seat and tell us who were those manufacturers who made that promise, and what was the promise, that was made. But I do not see the right hon. gentleman there, I do not think the Prime Minister is in his seat. Oh, I understand; Mr. Herridge must be in town, and his company is more interesting to the Prime Minister than the company of his colleagues. But, sir, we are discussing a most important matter. On Thursday last when we were discussing unemployment, the Minister of Labour was in his seat but the Prime Minister was not. Someone told me: "Herridge is in town." Yesterday we were discussing unemployment, the Prime Minister was not here. Herridge was in town! Herridge interests him more than the matter of unemployment. Perhaps the Prime Minister wants to hear the gossip as to how the St. Lawrence waterway treaty came to be defeated in Washington; that may be the big interest with him. We are discussing the most important matter of the session, the matter of unemployment,-unemployment created by his insane policy, but the right hon. gentleman is listening to gossip in some other room of the house. The captain is not on the dock. I think the attention of the house should be called to that. I am very sorry it happens that way, for I would like to have some answer to the very reasonable question that I have put, after reading excerpts from the speech delivered by the Prime Minister in the special session of 1930. But he is not here to answer; and if he were there would be no answer, for he always finds a way to evade answering reasonable questions put by members of this house. What was said then by the right hon. gentleman was most childish; he would have been most credulous to believe what was said to him by these manufacturers, promising to employ more men if the tariff were increased. Did they keep their word? No.
A little further on in the same speech the Prime Minister continued:
We propose therefore to provide that so far as may be reasonably possible the requirements of the 10.000,000 people living on the northern half of this continent shall be provided by Canadian producers.

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Pouliot
What happened? We find distress, especially among the farmers and labouring men. What the government did at the suggestion of the Prime Minister in 1930 was to raise the tariff without taking the trouble to study the effect in detail. They raised the tariff at the request of these people who were filling the corridors of this house and pressing the Prime Minister for an increase of tariff without any due consideration of the merits. He had power, he used it, but did he relieve unemployment? At that time the number of unemployed was about 100,000, one for each hundred of the population. It was very easy for Canada at that time to give relief to the poor. Municipalities were doing that without even the assistance of the provinces. The works done at that time were normal works. But little by little, step by step, the number of unemployed increased until now at least one-third of the citizens of Canada are unemployed. The first experiment in unemployment relief was to raise the tariff, on the assurance given by manufacturers that they would employ more men, 25,000 more they said, but the Prime Minister said that was not enough; he would provide employment for more than that.
That was the first step. What happened at the same time? The Dunning budget that had been prepared with a view to giving opportunity to the Canadian delegates to discuss trade matters with other countries was thrown aside. The Prime Minister came back from London with empty hands. He was unsuccessful at the conference of 1930 because he had no policy. Then came the session of 1931. After having cut off the hands of Canadian trade at the special session of 1930 he cut off the feet of Canadian trade at the session of 1931. Then we had that famous imperial conference of 1932. Well, the government bears a great burden of responsibility. I try to be fair, I do not put the blame so much on the other ministers as I do on the Prime Minister. The blame attaching to them is that they do not tell him to go at once and let some other minister -any one-be the captain of the ship in these stormy days. We have had enough of those experiments with the butcher knife or the axe. Tariffs are not to be dealt with in that way. It is an extremely delicate thing, and when considering the tariff it is most important to take every precaution, to be well informed, to weigh the pros and cons and thoroughly discuss the change that may be suggested. The government has no plan. Why do we have this blank cheque policy? It is because the government program is
blank; there is nothing to it. The Prime Minister decided nothing and waited until the last moment to urge the house to pass his legislation. All legislation should be carefully studied; that is most important. We have special rights as members of this house, rights that date back to the Magna Charta. Why were those rights put aside? It was because the government had no program at the time. In 1930 the government had no program except to raise the tariff; that was idealism. The Prime Minister said his party had a mandate to raise the tariff. Well, Mr. Speaker, many other matters were discussed during the campaign. The Prime Minister had a mandate to increase the price of butter, to the benefit of the producer. He had a mandate to bring prosperity to every home. That was wrhy the people elected him by such a large majority, but if the people had known what was to happen in the latter part of 1930 and in 1931, 1932, 1933 and until the present do you think so many would have voted to support the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite?
The right hon. gentleman always comes along with a new experiment. Why does he not succeed in the government of this country? The reason is very simple; it is because he has disregarded and discarded Liberal policies. He put them aside and said, "Now we will try experiments." He was not qualified; he was not sufficiently prepared to make the change by himself. Sometimes I have the greatest commiseration for his ministers, some of whom are very able. They have no opportunity to be heard, because the power behind the throne is in Washington. I regret that very much. The members of the cabinet are in a very humiliating position; they are not equally gifted, but some are very able men. I am sorry that their opinion does not count. It is Herridge who bosses everything; the Prime Minister; instead of listening to the sound advice of his ministers, listens to gossip from Washington. I am sorry for those who suffer as a result; I am sorry for the workingmen, the farmers and men in every other walk of life-

We must consider this
legislation in its true light, and we must realize that all hon. members will be submitted to the same judgment for their actions in this House of Commons. We must act fairly and give the right hon. gentleman credit for his sincerity. I believe he is sincere, but I regret from the bottom of my heart that some hon. gentlemen opposite and a section of the press have paid him compliments so high that they have gone to his

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. McIntosh
head. We must consider matters calmly. We are not in a position where we may make light of them.
When I think of the unemployment problem I am reminded that every day 1 pass a building on Elgin street which for a time was used as a church and is now used as a shelter for the unemployed. Why is it so? It is because the state is unable to take care of the unemployed, and private charity has to give assistance to the needy. I take this opportunity to make a statement which this week is of particular significance, namely that the church is giving that assistance. The unemployed men were in that church because they found shelter there. They are expecting and hoping for better times, and that sooner or later they may secure work.
Do we not remember that at the special session, of 1930 from his seat in the house the Prime Minister said, " Those people do not ask for charity; they want work. We will not give them charity; we will give them work." How is it so many of those men are on direct relief? They are on relief because the government has no policy but is still operating under a blank cheque policy. What has been done under that policy? Money has been advanced to Newfoundland; private firms have received guarantees or support from the government; the state has come to the relief of individuals-conditions which, under a well governed state, should not exist.
I shall not speak at greater length in this connection but shall ask hon. gentlemen opposite to curtail all further laudatory exaggerations of the Prime Minister, and give him an opportunity again to become what he was when he acted as leader of the opposition. In those days he was a simpler man, but they have spoiled him. They have made him different from what he was, and they are responsible. I hope some day they will understand that in this House of Commons flattery is useless, and that members of the House of Commons are above it. Perhaps if hon. members opposite would realize the truth of what I am saying we might some day have from the government sound policies sufficient to meet present conditions.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, in continuing the
debate on this vicious piece of legislation may I say that I want to touch upon three phases thereof before the house. One is that if the government had a constructive trade policy we would not at this time be dealing with an unemployment problem. Some may say that because of a world situation we would have
unemployment anyway. Well, to a certain extent that may be true, but the volume of unemployed we have to-day would not exist in Canada if we had a constructive national and international progressive trade policy. Secondly, I believe that the unemployment dilemma in which the government finds itself after four years of attempted rule has come about largely through its trade policy, and because the path it has been pursuing politically and otherwise has been absolutely unsound
First, with regard to trade it might be well to say that the condition now existing in Canada did not always obtain. In 1929 our trade with the United Kingdom was valued at approximately $625,009,000. In 1930, a year afterwards, it had dropped to $472,000,000. In that year the Liberals left office. Then, in 1931, when the present administration was getting down to business, trade dropped to $370,000,000, in 1932, to $290,000,000 and in 1933 to the paltry sum of $271,000,000. These figures indicate a drop in trade from over $600,000,000 to about $300,000,000, or a drop in the ratio of two to one.
In 1896 when the Liberal government came into power under Laurier, what did the Liberals of that day do? They inaugurated and put into effect a progressive empire trade policy. Although the policy was opposed by Conservatives of that day, notwithstanding the opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and those who followed him attempted and succeeded in one of the greatest pieces of trade reconstruction that had ever been known in the history of the empire, and Canada benefited immensely from that move. In 1896 Canada had a trade with the United Kingdom valued at only about $99,000,000, but in 1911 after fifteen years of Laurier rule, it had reached about $250,000,000, or about two and a half times as much. In 1925, when the Liberals were in power, the trade had reached $548,000,000. Hon. members will note that under Liberal rule, trade with the United Kingdom rose from $99,000,000 to over $600,000,000. To-day it is down to about one-third of that; in other words, two-thirds of that trade has been destroyed. Is it any wonder we have unemployment? Is it any wonder we have about 1,300,000 people living on relief in this country and that we have thousands and thousands of unemployed, that the family life of Canada has been to a large extent disintegrated, and that we have the growth of ideas politically in many ways that are not for the good of this country? I do not think we need wonder at the conditions that have come about.
Take our trade with the United States. We find practically the same story. In 1929,

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. McIntosh
when the Liberals were in power under my right hon. leader, our trade with the United States amounted to $1,381,000,000; in 1930, $1,383,000,000. In 1931 it started to go down, the minute this government came into power, dropping in that year to $900,000,000. In 1932 it dropped to 8600,000,000. There was a continual dropping and dropping, and with unemployment increasing until we are in the position we are in to-day. In 1933, just a year ago, our trade with the United States was $380,000,000. In other worde hundreds of millions of our trade with the United States have disappeared just as hundreds of millions of our trade with the United Kingdom have disappeared.
This decline in international trade means a decrease in national business, and a serious reduction in national business means the destruction of employment and the introduction of unemployment until by degrees we find ourselves in the position we are in at the present time.
What about Canada's total trade-not our trade with the United Kingdom, not our trade with the United States, but Canada's trade with the whole world? That is an important thing to consider because the world is the ultimate economic unit, the ultimate trade unit, and if we do not measure up in world trade, then of course unemployment will appear and the financial and commercial state of the nation will go from bad to worse.
In 1929 Canada's position in world trade was a phenomenal one. Our trade in that year amounted to over $2,600,000,000. In
1930	it dropped to $2,400,000,000. But note the drop when this government came into power and on up to the present time. In
1931	it had dropped to SI,700,000,000; in 1932 to $1,100,000,000, and in 1933, last year, it had dropped to about $900,000,000, or about one-third of what it was in 1929. That does not take into consideration the fact that in 1933 the gold value of the dollar was only 87 per cent of its gold value in 1932, so really we ought to deduct ten per cent from the figure I have given for 1933, and if we do that we find that our world trade in that year amounted to merely $800,000,000.
Looking at it in another way, if we let the total trade of Canada in 1929 equal 100, and we measure our trade by that yardstick, we see that in 1932 our trade had dropped to 34 per cent, whereas world trade measured by the same yardstick dropped to only about 39 per cent. In other words Canada's trade dropped five per cent more than world trade. Surely that makes it plain that all the ills that have

come upon us have not been because of a world situation that has developed.
So, Mr. Speaker, we find that the causes of this destruction of trade are to be found in tariffs and trade restrictions, in war debts and the cessation of international lending, but above and beyond all may I say that in my humble opinion tariffs have done more to destroy world trade and bring about the unemployment situation in which we now find ourselves to-day than any other factors. The export trade of Canada in 1929 amounted to $1,300,000,000; in 1930, $1,100,000,000, and in 1933 it had dropped to $480,000,000. There is the trade picture of Canada in its relation to the whole world. I have given it to the house in relation to the United Kingdom and in relation to the United States, and the all-compelling thought is simply this, that the trade policy of this government has been a failure. Its tariff policy too is absolutely wrong. No country like Canada can prosper and grow and develop under a prohibitive tariff policy. In the history of Canada before confederation and from confederation down to 1878, and from 1878 to 1896, and from 1896 to 1911, and from 1911 down to the present time, anyone who cares to read will find that a prohibitive tariff simply destroys Canadan trade, interferes with business, and gradually brings us into a position where we have great unemployment and always a position that is not in any way favourable.
Second, what about the unemployment policies of the present government in 1930, the last time an appeal was made to the Canadian public? You will find that it gave many pledges and promises to the people of Canada-pledges and promises prophetic of its political doom. These pledges have already been put on Hansard, but with a federal election coming on-since we have come to the fifth session of this parliament-I think it is only well to again put on Hansard these widely-proclaimed pledges and promises, for I believe the Canadian people can read and re-read them with profit. They tell the whole story, and the whole story is this: The present government got into power by promises and pledges which they have not carried out. They have not measured up to their promises and pledges, but have done the opposite, so that to-day Canada is faced with the most serious unemployment situation it ever had. In 1930 they promised by a system of prohibitive protection to develop our natural resources. How much have they done, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to develop our natural resources by prohibitive protection? I leave it to the parliamentarians and to the Canadian people to answer whether there has been any develop-

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. McIntosh
ment worth speaking of. Consequently that pledge has fallen dowTn.
They-the Conservative high command- also pledged that by a system of high protection they would develop our agricultural and industrial life and keep the consumers from exploitation. Well, the deplorable story that we have heard in this house during the last few weeks, and the exploiting evidence that has been adduced in the committee inquiring into the spread between the price the producer receives and the price the consumer pays, furnishes a direct contradiction of the pledge of the federal government that it would by a protective tariff protect our consumers from exploitation. Had the pledge been put the other way, it would have been the truth. If they had said that by a system of high protection or prohibitive tariffs the consumers would be exploited from coast to coast, that would have foretold exactly what has taken place.
They also pledged to develop agriculture, the live stock industry, the dairy industry, and to bring about stabilization of economic conditions; to build up foreign trade and empire trade, and at the same time to have these compensating advantages extend to all other avenues of public life.
There are their pledges, practically seven or eight, and not one of which has been kept. Not one piece of constructive development has taken place in our Canadian national life in the last four years, no development of our natural resources, no building up of agriculture, no development of world trade or empire trade, and no stabilization of economic conditions. Not one of those pledges has been worked out, and in that we find the explanation of the fact that we have over one million people on relief in Canada to-day. What a record!
May I just touch for a moment or two upon some of the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and see how they measure up with present conditions and with this iniquitous bill now before parliament. What did he say? At Edmonton he said that he would face unemployment at once. But he has not faced unemployment at once or at any other time. He may have faced it but that is all he has done, he has not solved it. Again he said: "I accept the challenge." Any man who is a real man will accept a challenge and face it; he will bring about a condition of affairs so that the challenge will not hold goodi-will, in fact disappear. But the challenge is as good to-day as it ever was, showing that the Prime Minister has not accepted it in the real sense. He has thrown it aside and the challenge is there still, even worse than it was
in 1930. What did he say at Chatham, New Brunswick? He said: "Put me into power and this bogy of unemployment will be destroyed." Has the bogy of unemployment been destroyed? Has it? It is bigger to-day than it ever was. In 1930 it was but a molehill but in 1934 it has become a mountain. The condition is more serious than ever. What did he say at Moncton? He said: "The Conservative party is going to find work or perish in the attempt." I think it will perish in the attempt.
This unemployment problem is the biggest problem facing Canada to-day. The Liberals are going to challenge the government on its lack of policy in not facing this question. Make no mistake about it, the unemployment problem is here and must be solved. If this government cannot solve it, then the Canadian people will soon see that a government is put into power that can solve it. We, the official opposition will watch in all seriousness and with all vigilance every move made by this government between, now and election day. We will watch the government to see what policy it brings forth and how it is going to manipulate vainly to get out of the position in which it now finds itself. The only thing the government can do is to bring down a real policy, a policy that will build up trade, relieve unemployment and restore the confidence of the Canadian people.
According to the Ottawa Citizen of July 14, 1930, the Prime Minister said that he would solve the unemployment problem and if he did not he would ask his supporters from Quebec and other members of his party to put him out of office. He has not solved this problem and the members from Quebec have not voted him out of office. The members from the other provinces have not voted him out of office. They sit there day after day in a docile manner; they see the lack of policy with regard to unemployment, with regard to trade, with regard to finance and with regard to everything, yet they continue to vote to keep this government in power. They are opposing themselves to the promises made years ago by the Prime Minister.
What did the Prime Minister say at Vancouver? He said: "I will see that my promises are carried out or I will go out of power trying to do so." There is no doubt that those promises have not been carried out and may I say there is no doubt that he will go out of power trying to carry them out. At Winnipeg the Prime Minister said that he would meet the unemployment problem or perish in the attempt. At Sarnia he said that Canada

was in a critical condition. At that time the condition of Canada was not comparable with the condition to-day. If Canada was in a critical condition on July 17, 1930, Canada is in a much more critical condition to-day. He said: "Unemployment exists,"-unemployment to-day is tenfold and twentyfold what it was then; what is the government going to do about it? Proceeding, he said: "-on a scale which never before was known in the history of this country." To-day we have unemployment on a scale never before known in the history of Canada and yet this government is standing idly by without a policy. It has been completely beaten in its attempt to put Canadian industry and commerce on its feet.
At Montreal the Prime Minister said: "The first duty of a Canadian government is to provide work for Canadians." If that is the first duty of a Canadian government then this government has not measured up to its primary duty. It has not furnished work for Canadians. It has not furnished work in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario, in the west or in British Columbia. What we want to-day is mobility or activity in exchange. If we get that we will prosper, if we do not get it, we cannot prosper. Canada to-day is without a policy, without leadership, without direction and without determination that something tangible must be done for the Canadian people. We have a government which does not inspire the Canadian people and the result is that conditions are not improving as quickly as they should.
Without dealing further with the promises made by the Prime Minister, may I say that the Liberal party has a policy with regard to unemployment. They had a policy in 1896 and unemployment disappeared in a year or so. When Laurier came into power in 1896 the Liberals opened up the great west and delivered this country from bondage. Laurier made a greater Canada and stood for a greater dominion. He gave scope to thought and action in this country and the result is that to-day we have a Canada from coast to coast. Again, when the Liberals came into power under my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1922 we had unemployment, but it lasted only a year or so until the Liberal policies were under way. Unemployment disappeared like mist before the morning sun. For eight years Canada had development, progress and prosperity. When I make the statement that the Liberals have a policy which if put into effect will solve the problem of unemployment, I am merely stating what is proved by history. It is not guess work, it is a fact. This statement is in accordance

with the record of Liberalism in Canadian history.
What is the policy of the Liberal party with regard to unemployment? I assure the house that it is not a policy of prohibitive tariffs. Such tariffs have destroyed Canadian public life and business, both national and international. The time has come when we must have something different in this country. I do not intend to touch upon tariffs at any great length but I should like to give one example. The importation of mowers and binders affects all the farmers in this country. Under Mr. Borden the tariff on these articles was twelve and a half per cent; under Mr. Meighen it was twelve and a half per cent, but under the Liberal administration of the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King it was only six per cent, ome-half of what it was under Borden and one-half of what it was under Meighen. But what did this government do in this connection? What they did is known all over Canada. Is it any wonder that agriculture has been demoralized, is it any wonder that our farmers are discouraged when we realize what this government has done? Under Mr. Bennett the tariff on these articles was raised to twenty-five per cent, just four times what it was under Liberal rule. This is what is known as prohibitive tariff legislation and it is such legislation that destroys business and brings about conditions such as we have in Canada at the present moment.
What is the policy of the Liberal party with regard to this unemployment problem, the most crucial problem confronting Canada to-day? The Liberals always had a policy and they always will have a policy because the Liberal party is the party of progress, of idealism, of power, of determination and advancement. Those who stand by that party as did Laurier and the other leaders of Liberalism, will always be in the van of progress.
Now here is the policy of the Liberal party on this question of unemployment. The Liberal party stands for the liberation of external trade. That means that trade is in bondage at the present time, and the Liberal party will take external trade, international trade, overseas trade, out of bondage, out of slavery, and take the Canadian people out of slavery along with it. The Liberal party, in other words, believes that trade is the basis of industrial and commercial development, and that Canada needs trade. Heaven knows she needs trade, and more than that she needs a new government and new leadership at the same time. Moreover, the Liberal party will promote trade with all nations, and negotiate

Relief Act, 1934~Mr. McIntosh
trade agreements with every country willing to trade with this country on a reciprocal basis. The Liberal party will abolish extravagant increases in the tariff made by the present administration, which increases have had the effect of strangling trade, exploiting commerce and consumers and robbing the railways of business. The Liberal party will abolish all unwarranted extra taxes on imports, such as the exchange and dumping duties imposed by the present administration. The Liberal party will put an end to the making and altering of tariffs by executive action. The Liberal party will substitute stability for uncertainty in the administration of customs affairs, and will continue the Liberal policy of a British preference, by means of lowering the tariff to Great Britain rather than by a percentage increase in the tariff against foreign countries. The Liberal party will concede to British imports a real preference, and by so doing build up empire trade once more. Further than that, the Liberal party will make it possible for this country to trade with every nation in the world.
But let me go further. The Liberal party stands not only for the liberation of external trade but, in a complementary manner, it stands for the liberation of internal trade, because national trade and international trade go hand in hand. They are complementary; one supplements the other, and if you have one in the larger sense you will have the other, provided you pursue the right policy. And so the Liberal party stands firm for the liberation of internal trade. That means, just as it meant in connection with external trade, that our national or internal trade is also in bondage, in slavery, shackled hand and foot, so that it is impossible for it to fimction, and the consequence of that is that ten million Canadians are practically in poverty, and industrial stability and development from coast to coast is a thing of the past.
Now what is the Liberal policy, in its exact words, with regard to the liberation of internal trade? Here it is:
The Liberal party will seek to end' artificial price control and agreements in restraint of trade. Price-fixing by agreements restricts and hampers trade internally, and the internal trade of the country has become honeycombed and enmeshed by secret understandings and agreements.
How can national trade grow and flourish under such conditions? Yet this government, and those who sit behind thorn, have allowed a condition such ns I have described to grow up until trade is strangled both inside and outside of Canada. In addition to these two 74726-119
important, planks in 'the Liberal party's policy of building up trade -and smashing unemployment, destroying it for good in this country, we have the Liberal party standing firm on the development of the primary in-diuatries, on the development of agriculture, mining, lumbering, the fisheries, and on the development of all other primary industries. Unless we free these industries basically we cannot expect secondary industries like manufacturing to prosper, and unless we make it possible for our basic industries, our primary industries and secondary industries :to prosper, we shall not have much prosperity in this country, nor shall we get very far away from the unemployment condition that has ominously reared its ugly form in our land since 1930.
The Liberal party stands for the development of our primary industries along same, constructive land progressive lines. The Liberal party will see that the .right degree of democracy is instilled into every industry, whether basic or secondary, and may I quote its policy on this important point, "The Liberal party believes that industrial reconstruction is the problem of the future". It has not yet dawned on .this government as the problem of thie future, for there has been no industrial reconstruction so far as this gov-eromemf is concerned,-simply industrial destruction. Further than that, the Liberal party will seek in industrial relations, as opportunity offers, to give to workers and consumers a large share in the government of industry, control of industry -by those who work therein, thereby bringing about satisfactory labour conditions and giving a lead to reconstruction not only in an industrial way but also with respect to labour, from coast to coast.
I am told that I have but ten minutes in which to conclude my remarks, and in that ten minutes I wish to deal with the bill before us. The preamble gives us an idea of what the bill ought to be, but it does not in reality tell .us what the measure actually contemplates. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this bill should not foe before pariiamient. this bill is no honour to the Canadian dominion. This bill is no honour to a man who calls himself a British citizen, a Canadian, or a member nation of the great British Empire. This^ bill does not appeal to any man who has in him the blood of freedom and liberty that characterized our forefathers, who had to build up the empire, and whose descendants are calling upon us to-day to maintain this same liberty and freedom.

Oaths of Allegiance Act

As far as I am comoeamed, I am not afraid to take a stand on this bill. I repudiate every word, every phrase, every sellable, every clause, and every paragraph of this bill, as far as its import on Canadian partUamenitary and public life is concerned. lit is not in line with Canadian democracy; it is not in line with British freedom or liberty; it is opposed to all these, and so far as these features are concerned I am opposed to the bill, whether every' man in this house votes for it or noit. On one occasion I heard him tell of a subscriber in one of the Oarolinas who had contributed $50,000 towards the program.

Speaking for the Prime Minister and myself I must object to those secular concerts being broadcast on Sunday afternoons. The Minister of Marine has said that the people of Canada were very much pleased with the different concerts. I am very much afraid that the minister has had his head in the air instead of having his ear to the ground, because there is no question in my mind that the concerts and the reception in Canadian radio to-day is not as good as when Commander Edwards did the whole thing for a much smaller sum of money than this commission is costing the country.

I do not wish to enter into a discussion of this matter, but I should like to point out that there are some people in Canada who would be very glad to wreck the Canadian Radio Commission. I do not think we should be over critical of an institution which has had very little time to perform a very great task, without having much precedent to follow. It was practically a new business and had to be organized from its inception. On the whole I think the com-

mission has done very well. I believe that there is considerable agitation throughout the country to try to upset the commission and get the whole thing back again into private hands, but while hon. members have every right to question every expenditure and be critical, I think we ought to go a little slow in our wholesale criticism of the radio commission. Personally I think it has been a great improvement. The programs are very much better than they were, and in another year I believe that there will be much greater improvement. I for one have every sympathy for the commission.
