The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. 42, respecting relief measures.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, when the house
rose at six o'clock I had dealt with two of the angles of the bill before the house, namely, the question of trade and trade policy upon which depends in the last analysis employment or unemployment in any nation and, second, the question of unemployment, its causes in a general way and the Liberal trade policy which if put into effect in Canada will surely destroy and put to rout the unemployment conditions which exist in this country ait the present time. There is a third aspect of the measure with which I want to deal. We are told in the preamble of this bill thait it is proposed to furnish financial aid to the provinces by way of guarantees, advances and loans; second, to further the unhampered prosecution of direct relief and a works program in order to help the unemployment situation and, third, to maintain dominion and provincial credit. These are three worthy objectives and I have no fault to find with any bill trying to arrive at any one of them. From a practical point of view I would be willing to support the government in its desire to give financial assistance to the provinces, to further direct relief and to uphold the credit of the dominion and the provinces.
However, when I go beyond the preamble and come to the blank cheque principle and the further principle, closely allied to it, of destroying the power of parliament, then I am opposed to the bill. As far as the principle of the blank cheque is concerned, this brings us face to face with the question of the control of parliament over expenditure. I should like to put on record the position of the Liberal party with regard to this important question. I have in my hand a book entitled "Evolution of the Dominion of Canada" by Edward Porritt. This is a very important publication and on page 149 appears some of the things for which the Liberal party stood for in days gone by. They are:
Reform in the method of sale of crown lands.
Abolition of customs houses and duties on imports.
An elected legislative council.
[Mr. Rhodes.}
There has been an abolition of nearly all the legislative councils in Canada. The Liberal party also stood for:
Election by county and municipal councils of all county and municipal officers.
An extension of the electoral franchise.
No expenditure of public money without the control of the legislature.
Representation according to population.
Abolition of pensions to government officials.
Canadian commerce and commercial intercourse -with other nations to be entirely under the control of the legislature.
The legislature to have power to alter or repeal any act or charter, imperial or otherwise, affecting only Canada, which the imperial parliament itself might alter or repeal.
I should like to refer to the one paragraph, no expenditure of public money without the control of the legislature. The bill now before us is designed .to spend public money and no figure is incorporated in the bill. We can spend hundreds or thousands, millions or hundreds of millions, and if we pass this bill we shall be relinquishing the power of parliament to control revenue a historic principle for the preservation of which the Liberal party in days gone by opposed the Conservatives. It was as a result of that opposition that we have that principle incorporated in our constitution. But this government is taking the same stand which the party it represents took one hundred years ago with respect to this very important fundamental. Hon. gentlemen opposite are opposing the very foundation of parliamentary government and of constitutional rule in Canada, and as a Liberal I am obliged to stand up and oppose such a course. I oppose the Prime Minister, every minister of the cabinet and every member behind the cabinet in my contention for this principle. Let me show the attitude of the Tory party throughout the history of Canada towards this important principle; you will see that where the party stood one hundred years ago iit stands to-day. It has made no progress- absolutely none. At page 111 of the same work to which I have referred there appears the following:
The claim for responsible government was conceded in 1841. The concession was withdrawn in 1843, but was completely and finally conceded in 1849. Its first and its final concessions were due, not to anything actually stated in the act of 1840, although that memorable act was the key to all the constitutional freedom now enjoyed by all the dominions. They were due to the statesmanship and democratic spirit of Sydenham, Bagot, and Elgin, three of the four governors-general who were in office from 1839 to 1850, and also, it is important to note, to the new policy literally forced on Downing street by the

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Duguay
Liberals of Upper and' Lower Canada, who were in control of the legislative assembly of the United Provinces, during the first decade of the constitution of 1840.
So that where the Conservative party stood in 1840, in 1841 and in 1848 the Conservatives of the present day stand; and the Prime Minister's attitude is directly opposed to the stand taken by Ragot, by Sydenham, by Elgin and by Durham, yes, by all constitutional leaders. I say therefore that the right hon. gentleman is diametrically opposed to the parliamentary principles of liberty and freedom on which this great dominion is based.
Le me go further. At page 137 of the same work I find the following:
A disposition to observe constitutional usages and practices was never characteristic of the Tories of the Family Compact groups in Upper and Lower Canada.
That disposition has never been characteristic of them, and it is not characteristic of the Conservative party in this dominion at the present time. They are out to undermine responsible government and to destroy parliamentary control in Canada; and I fancy that when the country is appealed to, this constitutional problem, together with other problems that will evolve as this parliament proceeds, will receive the consideration of the people. I have no doubt about that, and I am satisfied to abide by the decision of the electorate. The author says further, with reference to the Conservatives:
They were a law to themselves, as was sufficiently proved by their ejection of Mackenzie from the assembly at Toronto. They again ignored constitutional usage in the crisis over the rebellion losses bill. They organized many petitions against the bill: but instead of presenting these petitions to the assembly, or to the legislative council, in accordance with the usage at Westminster, they addressed them to Elgin personally. This unconstitutional course was obviously adopted with the design of bringing about a collision between the governor general and his ministry and the assembly.

By the way, I warn him to be on his guard, because Mr. Taschereau may, one of these days, send him a little note reproaching him for insulting the people of Quebec. I have had some experience in this respect. The right hon. leader of the opposition strongly criticized the provincial governments in connection with the unemployment problem. I quite agree with him in this matter. May I state, sir, that this question was brought up in the house, even before the Conservative party came into office.- An attempt is being made to have the people believe that the unemployment crisis prevails only since the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is at the helm of the country's affairs. May I point out that, on March 31, 1930, the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) introduced in the house the following resolution :
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment.
Therefore, the unemployment problem existed in 1930, before the Conservative party assumed power.
What did the Prime Minister of the day reply?
On April 3, the right hon. Mr. King stated:
We have no right to state that an unemployment crisis exists in this country.
On April 8, this motion was defeated by a vote of 100 against 81. All Liberals voted against extending help to the unemployed.
However, a general election took place and in the course of the summer the present leader of the opposition toured the whole of Canada. He became aware that the unemployment crisis which prevailed had spread more than he had thought, the fact is, sir, as all are aware, that when hon. members opposite are in office, they are not interested in finding out what are the needs of the people, their only aim is to maintain themselves in power and cater to their friends. The leader of the opposition became aware then that an employment problem did exist. What remedy did he bring to bear? He proposed that a commission be appointed. Fortunately, the people were not deceived by this commission, for they elected the present Prime Minister
Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Duguay

who immediately, in 1930, summoned parliament for the purpose of enacting measures to relieve unemployment.
In September, 1930, the government appropriated 820.000,000 toward relieving unemployment. What attitude did the Quebec premier take in this connection? He contended that the Dominion government had not appropriated a sufficient amount to relieve unemployment, though he, himself, had proclaimed in the course of the 1930 election that there were no unemployed in his province. Why? Simply to be in unison with his very dear friend, the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King.
The right hon. leader of the opposition four years later discovers irregularities in the distribution of moneys to relieve unemployment. Everybody knows that the Dominion government could take no other means than to have the distribution done by the provinces and municipalities. The irregularities were committed by the provincial governments. In the cases quoted in the house, by the leader of the opposition, we concluded that the principal irregularities took place in Quebec. Why? Because, unfortunately for the Quebec people, the leader of the provincial government is a Liberal.
May I, sir, read what the hon. leader of the opposition stated in the house on January 29, 1934:
Everyone who knows what has taken place with respect to relief moneys in the provincial elections which have been held is aware of the manner in which public moneys have been used by the governments of those provinces or of the dominion in order to give employment to large numbers of men during the period of elections. I am to understand these are the only purposes for which this power has been usefl in the four years during which relief measures have been on the statute books, and in the two years during which this section has been included in those measures. Why then, may I ask, do we need this section inserted again for this year? With all the other powers the ministry have had heretofore and now possess, what grounds can the government urge for again asking parliament to insert this particular clause in the section?
I want to read the entire section, so that the minister will see the force of my remarks. So far as the opposition are concerned, we have no desire to prevent the government from being in a position to take any step that may be necessary to meet an emergent condition, and from having power for which they can give reasonable grounds. But we do very strongly oppose departing altogether from the practice of parliament with respect to legislation, and handing over to the governor in council a power to legislate which belongs, and ought to belong only, to parliament, because that is what it means when the governor in council is given power to pass orders with respect to peace, order and good government, notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law. That phrase is broad enough to cover legislation on anything. The minister tells us it has been used only to prohibit the export of gold and to enable the securities of banks and insurance companies to be revalued. Let us see what the power would be which by this section the government would be given, apart from that given it by this objectionable clause. If that particular clause were struck out of this section to-day the section would read as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may,-
(a)	Upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon.-enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein; grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise; and in respect of such loans, advances and guarantees, may accept such security, enter into such agreements and generally do all such acts and things as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient in the public interest;
(b)	When parliament is not in session-
Then omitting the clause relating to peace, order and good government, and continuing:
-and at all times to take such measures as in his discretion may be deemed' necessary or advisable to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
Surely those powers which I think go much too far, are comprehensive enough to enable the governor in council, in addition to existing legislation, to deal with any critical situation when parliament may not be in session. But in the circumstances, if the government say they used those additional extensive powers and will take the responsibility of asking parliament for them, so far as we are concerned we are prepared not to oppose such action. We do, however, oppose very strongly the reintroduction into this measure of a clause which is most objectionable, which was enacted only by use of the closure in 1931, and was dropped in the year 1932. I refer to the section respecting peace, order and good government.
May I give another reason why that particular clause should not be inserted? The government has taken credit to itself for having dropped the following clause:
Loan or advance money to or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking.

Mr. Chairman, the very fact that the government proceeded under this part of section 2 on only three occasions is at least considerable evidence that they would take action under the section only in cases where it became apparent that in order to avoid a great major difficulty speedy action should be taken. While I am in agreement with the remarks of the right hon. gentleman with respect to the sanctity of the rights of parliament in matters of this kind, yet I think every hon. member wijl agree that during the last few years we have watched a changing world. In Canada we cannot always be the authors of our own course, or even nearly so, but rather at times speedy action has to be taken. Occasion may arise, even during a recess of parliament, when by reason of events beyond our control action might have to be taken before a special session of parliament could be convened. I say again that I am not by any means unacquainted with the laws and ordinances which have grown up, some incorporated into statute law, and some by reason of long practice and usage, which preserve to parliament its rights. But I am also aware of the fact that in times like these-and I hope it will not be necessary- the executive or the government might have to turn to this authority in order to take speedy action in connection with matters touching vitally the business of the country.
If the right hon. leader of the opposition is really fearful that the government will during the recess of parliament take undue

powers under this section and act without good and sufficient reason, I can only repeat that in the past in my judgment the government has not acted in that way, and I do not think it will do so between now and the next sitting of parliament. I feel that while at times on the part of one party there may be a desire in this chamber to survive over another party-a principle which seems very closely identified with political activities in Canada-yet I feel that the real desire of all members is to adopt such legislation as is best calculated to meet and to overcome the difficulties which to-day and for some years past have confronted Canada.

The minister has said that in the past the government have never used in an objectionable manner the powers conferred upon them by relief legislation, and that to be sure of the future we should rely on what has happened in the past. It is because we do not believe that parliament has been treated fairly in the past under relief legislation that we have objections to granting anew the powers asked in this bill. A glaring instance is afforded us in the orders in council laid on the table of the house a few days ago concerning the guarantees of the government with respect to the marketing of wheat. The first order in council is the one by virtue of which this country became responsible to seven banks for moneys advanced by them to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited for the marketing of wheat, and particularly including advances for the purchases of wheat or other grains deemed necessary to secure the advantageous sale of such grains already delivered or to be delivered. That order in council was passed on September 12, 1931. It is very interesting to read the order in council and to learn what preceded it. The order in council reads in part as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated 11th September, 1931, from the Minister of Finance, recommending that, in pursuance of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, and of an undertaking on behalf of the government, made before the session of parliament at which the said act was passed, to implement by legislation the recommendation hereinafter set out, the governor in council guarantee repayment.
And so forth. So during the whole session of 1931 the country had been engaged to the banks to guarantee the payments of these moneys by an undertaking preceding the session, which undertaking the government had pledged themselves to implement by legisla-

Relief Act, 1934
tion during the session. Was it treating parliament fairly not to introduce legislation into parliament in order to implement that undertaking? But instead the relief act was passed in July or August taking all the powers to do anything under the sun, and the government waited until September to do by order in council what should have been done by legislation, the confirming of an agreement entered into before the session of parliament. If that is treating parliament fairly I do not see why we should continue to exist as a parliamentary and legislative body.
The preamble of the present bill states the reasons why it is needed. It says:
Whereas the provinces may require further assistance in carrying out necessary relief measures and in meeting financial conditions as the same may arise; and whereas in such event it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as the governor in council may deem expedient; and whereas it is necessary to make provision for further expenditure for relief purposes under the Department of National Defence and the Department of the Interior; and whereas for these and similar purposes the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of such relief measures and the maintenance of the credit of the dominion and the provinces thereof should he vested in the governor in council;
All these purposes can be met by the various sections of the bill, excluding the one to which we mostly object, that relating to peace, order and good government. There is nothing in the preamble which justifies the insertion of these words which were eliminated from the preceding bill. I think that on further consideration the minister will drop that clause from the bill.

Each of us can speak only of conditions as they come under his observation and as are indicated by such records as are available, but my view is that conditions certainly are improving. In connection with the business with which I am associated and in the public office which I hold I have considerable opportunity to observe the state of business conditions. I know there are some who will not admit they are improving, who do not want to admit it. There is a class of people in this country who I believe would suffer a very severe disappointment if things did improve just now. There are some who are so mentally constituted, but perhaps they cannot help it. The fact remains, however, that from what information I can get I believe business is improving. As I said a few moments ago, certain countries have been content, perhaps with some anxiety, to invest the executives of their governments with powers which would have been unheard of ten years ago or before 1929 when world affairs, world business and world politics assumed an unprecedented degree of confusion and chaos which has been more or less apparent ever since. The only assurance I can give hon. members of the committee is that the government will take power under this section only when it is abundantly convinced that that power should be taken in order to maintain within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada. I rise however merely to point out to the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) that he is entirely in error when he assumes that there was any bad faith manifested to this parliament in connection with the guarantee given to the banks with respect to the account of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. The truth is, as perhaps he has gathered from the evidence given in the banking committee, that the guarantee was given in 1931 and has continued ever since and will continue until there is a liquidation of the accumulated surplus held by the Cooperative Producers Limited. That I think is fairly obvious. When he points out that the order in council to which he has just referred was prepared in the form in which it was, I would say to him that it was put in that form by the solicitor for the bankers' association, who thought there might be some uncertainty, and was of the opinion that it more clearly expressed the position of the banks in relation to the government if we put it in that form, and I informed him that there was no objection to it.
I would make it clear to the hon. gentleman that the transaction was as follows:	(1)
Advances made by the banks to the organization. (2) The guarantee given to the bank by the government, which could not in terms mention a specific sum. That, I think, will be found in the evidence given the other evening in the banking committee. (3) It continues from year to year, and the reason it was thought that it might be rewritten in the form in which it was ,was that there was some question as to the sufficiency of the language to carry over the liability from one year to the other and to make it clear that there was no uncertainty as to what was meant by the language employed; and the rewriting to which

the hon. gentleman has referred was done for the purpose of removing any doubts and at the instance of Mr. Henry T. Ross, secretary of the Canadian Bankers Association, with whom I considered it, and subsequently with the Minister of Justice, who said that there was no reason why, if they felt that it made the matter clear, it should not be put in the form in which it is.
I can only say that in this relief measure there has been an effort to remove certain clauses which it was felt conferred upon the government larger powers than the house was of opinion, under present conditions, should be conferred upon them; and all those words to which the minister has referred as being in last year's legislation were removed from the present bill. But with respect to peace, order and good government, if the right hon. gentleman is correct in saying that they add nothing to the existing language of other statutes, then it is abundant precaution which can do no harm. If on the other hand he feels that they might be necessary for the purpose of valuing securities, as he indicates was done, and which now fortunately for us is a matter that need give us no further consideration, inasmuch as the securities that were so valued have risen in value to a point far beyond that then expressed as a reasonable value, in that instance we were but following the practice which prevailed in Great Britain as well as in the United States; because our own securities having been sold in large quantities at the express request of the governments of the day to the banks, it was unfair to ask the banks, for the purposes of their balance sheets, to value them at a figure very much lower than that at which they had bought them-and it was not buying that was taking place at any particular time before 1930 but that had taken place from time to time'- to enable the government to secure funds from the banks and make success a certainty with respect to the sale of securities.
With respect to the insurance companies, the matter can be put on this simple ground. The liabilities are liabilities maturing in the future, and the whole business of insurance is predicated on the assumption that the present reserve will be sufficient, on the values placed on them at the time they are purchased, to meet obligations that will mature at some future period of time. What we did was to follow the practice that obtained in the forty-eight states of the union, where the commissioners of insurance met together and, with one single exception, determined that that was the proper action to take. And it was taken in a subsequent year as well.

So far as the words "peace, order and good government" are concerned, the reason they appear in the statute in the form in which they do is that they are words used in our constitution. It is felt that they confer, in case of emergency, power to be exercised by the executive for the peace, order and good government of the country for the purpose indicated in the measure, a power that should be in the hands of any government in these days. I think it is rather unfair to say that the government of British Columbia have borrowed from this parliament the proposals they have made to their legislature, because had it been our example, the statute would have read in this form: that during the time that parliament is in recess the governor in council may make laws to be called ordinances, and then recite the whole twenty-nine articles of section 91 of the British North America Act. The statute in British Columbia recites seriatim the various items in section 92 of the British North America Act and declares that when the legislature is not in session the lieutenant governor in council may make ordinances which shall have the force of law. In other words, the legislature is abolished; the assembly is abolished. Now, I am sure the right hon. gentleman will not suggest that we have endeavoured to abolish parliament by the section that appears here, because these words have a well defined meaning; and having a meaning well defined by the courts it is, I think, only reasonable, to ensure this country against any unforeseen difficulties that may arise between now and the time parliament meets, that provision of this character should be inserted in the legislation. There have been limitations imposed which we were glad to impose, but on the other hand in view of the very circumstances to which the premier of British Columbia has referred as to the effects of outside influences on the life of that province, and when reputable members stand in their places in this house and point to external influences endeavouring to destroy the very institutions of the country, I think that even although it may be a repetition of what is found in other statutes, it is well to make assurance doubly sure by providing that the executive, shall have authority, between the time that such conditions might arise and parliament be called together, to make orders for the peace, order and good government of the country. That is as far as it goes. It is difficult to assure hon. gentlemen who will not be assured, but I should like to assure my hon. friends opposite that there is no desire

Relief Act, 1934
to act either as a usurper or a dictator. If when they allege that we so act they think that the task involves pleasure, they would only have to put in the hours per day that are put in with respect to the very matters to which they refer to see that all pleasure and all happiness and comfort disappear in dealing with problems of this character.

I suppose it adds nothing to it to say that if for a single moment it had been thought desirable, or if the question had been asked, I should have been only too glad to say that a guarantee had been given to the banks, because from the very start we had no hesitancy in saying that. From the time in 1930 when an effort was made by the western provinces to induce the dominion government to set up a wheat board, or to "peg the price", as it was called, of wheat at 70 cents, we never showed any hesitancy in making clear to the country through this house what had been done; and from that day to this we have made it perfectly clear what was done. I think we made it abundantly clear the other evening.
I will say this, and I hope it will not be misunderstood, that while parliament is the great court of the country, the court of inquest, which has a right to know everything that is done by its executive, yet in times of stress and strain and difficulty, when the government has to have recourse to many methods of dealing with problems of extreme gravity, until such time as they are concluded it is sometimes injudicious to discuss them publicly. It is not suggested, of course, that there is anything that should not be disclosed, but only that the time is not always most opportune to do it while the matter is pending. I quite appreciate the attitude taken by the hon. gentleman; it is the attitude any opposition would take, that in a matter of this kind, where the executive is exercising its power, it should as far as possible make the fullest disclosures to the house of everything that transpires. I say further-it is not a matter of importance, but my colleagues
Reliej Act, 1934

will bear me out in this-that many times during the last three years when matters have been under consideration I have been asked why I do not make a statement about them. The other evening, after the discussion in connection with the guarantee to the railway company and in connection with the sale of wheat, the question was asked: Why could not these things be said at the time? I only say to this committee, and I ask men of experience in business whether their experience does not bear out what I say, that at times nothing could be more fatal to the transaction of business than a public discussion of it before it is concluded. My glance happening to rest upon the face of one hon. member opposite recalls a certain transaction in the public interest which was about to be carried out in connection with a rather large public undertaking, and a premature discussion wrecked it. Those who are familiar with the story of the purchase of the Suez canal shares will recall what has been said in the accounts of the lives of statesmen of that day as to what would have happened had this transaction, which was dealt with by Disraeli and the Rothschilds, become a matter of public discussion before Disraeli was enabled to close it out as he did.
Now I add only this. There is no desire in any way to keep from this house or from this country any particulars of any transaction with which this government has been connected since it came into office, affecting the public interest, under these various relief measures or other statutes that conferred authority and, in my opinion, imposed responsibilities. Those responsibilities we have endeavoured to discharge in the manner we thought best for the country. It is possible that I or my colleagues may have been in error, but if at times we believed that it was not in the public interest to blazon these matters from the housetops and not to discuss them even in this house until such time as further progress had been made in connection with some of them, I think we adopted a course which sound business at least, by experience, has indicated to be the proper course in connection with ordinary transactions. I believe my hon. friend from Quebec East will find, in connection with the matter to which he referred, that it was made abundantly clear to this house from the inception of the transaction that the government had given a guarantee to the banks to enable the cooperative wheat producers to carry out the business for which they had appointed Mr. McFarland their general manager, and which has been
[M~. Bennett.]
carried on ever since. In 1928 the excessive crop brought about too great a carry-over of grain into future years, which has been reflected in the excess carry-over ever since, until this very day.
I make that statement because, if there has been any suggestion that in any sense there has been an endeavour either to deceive this house or keep anything from it, other than what we thought should be kept back at the moment for good public reasons, I should like the fullest investigation before any committee of the house, with witnesses called to establish that what was done was done with an eye to one single purpose, and that was to endeavour to ensure that this house and this country would have no reason to say that, through the failure on our part to do something, there had been a collapse of public confidence or a panic in connection with any of our institutions that might imperil what had been built up by many years of laborious effort on the part of the Canadian people.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) I think have failed to understand the force of my objection, or at any rate to answer it. Possibly I have not made myself clear. The Prime Minister stated that my objection was that this clause simply duplicated previous legislation; that, to use his words, it was a repetition of previous legislation, that it added nothing to existing statutes, and that for this reason there should be no objection to making doubly secure that which is already secure. That was not my point at all. It is not that it adds nothing to existing legislation; it is that it takes away existing legislation, takes away the protection which existing legislation gives to citizens of ths country with respect to innumerable matters. The government asks that notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may, when parliament is not in session, take all such measures within the competence of parliament as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to maintain peace, order and good government.
That language is as plain as day if one will stop to look at it. It means that notwithstanding all the laws that parliament has made, with regard to insurance companies, banks, railways or anything else one wishes to name, the government may when parliament is not in session, set aside all those laws and pass any orders in council it pleases so long as it cares to designate them as necessary for the peaoe, order and good government of

Relief Act, 1934
Canada. That is the power for which they are asking, and I say that power is setting parliament altogether at naught. It is doing away with parliament and what parliament exists for, namely to protect the citizens of this country in their rights and privileges.
I doubt very much if hon. members have even yet grasped the significance of this section. We listened to the Prime Minister speak of the necessity of doing things quietly, of times being troubled and of the need to give the government an opportunity quickly to deal with an emergency, and so on. For my part I am ready to give the minister any powers for which they ask provided they will set out in black and white the exact powers needed and are able to support their request on reasonable grounds. But that is not what they are asking for here. They are asking that notwithstanding the existence of any statute or law, once this parliament has prorogued the governor in council may legislate as he pleases with regard to anything, regardless of existing legislation. I say that the granting of such power has in itself a terrible unsettling effect upon the country. The banks and those who have relations with banks, for example, do not know whether some section of some act on which they rely for protection in their rights is going to be set at naught by some order in council pased under the heading of peace, order and good government. The same statement applies to insurance companies or to anything else one may wish to name. That is what is asked for and that is what we object to granting. We are not objecting to making security doubly secure where there is any danger of an untoward incident of any sort or of the government not having sufficient power to deal with any situation. We are objecting to the danger of taking away that protection which this parliament has placed around business and around its citizens their rights, liberties and privileges, by the laws it has passed; we object to any legislation whereby, notwithstanding existing laws and statutes, these laws and statutes may all be set at naught if the government think it desirable so to do in order to pass an order in council contrary to their provisions.
I say again to the minister that I hope he will not press for this power this session. His powers have been gradually extended in other clauses of this section. To indicate my desire to cooperate with the government, so far as I am concerned, I will not take exception to the amendment which has been moved by the minister, although it gives him additional power with regard to a matter as to which he has already given guarantees. Anything
for which the minister can give reasonable grounds in a concrete way will meet with a like reception; he will find the opposition perfectly ready, I think, to meet him in a cordial, cooperative way, but in the light of what may take place I do not think we can be expected willingly to allow the government to set aside, if it so desires, all the existing statutes and laws and remain free to legislate as it pleases when parliament is no longer in session, and when the ministry may no longer exist or may not have this House of Commons to reckon with when it comes to seeking the explanation of why these particular powers were made use of in the manner they were at a particular time.

Mr. McFarland began his operations on the Winnipeg market in the fall of 1930, I think in November. Would not it be the natural and logical thing to have the standing of his account given to parliament at the end of each grain year, that is July 31? I think this should be done in order to preserve some of the business ethics of government which they are now demanding of others- chain stores for example. I have never had much business experience but I know of the old saying that short accounts make long friends and long accounts make short friends. Why should not the government try to follow out this adage and give us a short account in order to preserve a long friendship? Where you have an account running for years you are bound to get into trouble. It is claimed sometimes that memos have not been made or have been lost, that this and that has not been put down or someone has died, and perplexities thus arise. I have not been worrying the Prime Minister with questions to-day; this is the first one I have asked.
I might say that I have been a wheat pool contract signer, although there are no contracts now. As a citizen of Canada I have a share in the line of credit being used and the guarantee given by the government. I am interested also as one who still patronizes the wheat pool, even though there are no contracts. I do not think it is exacting or unreasonable to ask the government to let us have a statement up to the end of each crop year. Surely to goodness we could not ask anything more modest than that. I am in the position of my hon. friend to my right (Mr. Lapointe); my constituents are asking me for information about this. If this thing is allowed to run indefinitely there is bound to be trouble at the end. Someone will have to clean up the whole thing and it may not be our friends opposite; it may be some other government, even a government of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. To do this would be recognizing just a little of the business principles which actuate people in carrying on their own business.

I imagine the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) is just as well acquainted as I am with the facts in connection with the guaranteeing of wheat in western Canada during the last four years. There was a government which guaranteed the pool before this government came into the picture. The Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta governments saw fit to come to the rescue of the pools in 1929 and 1930. There was no disposition on the part of those governments at that time to conceal from the electorate or the taxpayers the position of things. It was well known during the whole [DOT] activities to what extent the governments were guaranteeing. In fairness to the hon. member for Melville, I must admit that no ill effects came from that information being given out. I cannot say whether there would be the same result if the information now asked for were given to the committee. My perambulations through western Canada were considerable for the six months before I left to come to Ottawa-I may say that I took part in the Mackenzie by-election-and in all my perambulations I did not meet one farmer who asked me how the government stood one way or the other. It is not very often that hon. members opposite agree that I am fair, but in this instance I must make that statement.
We must admit that there was a time when you could not sell wheat on the Winnipeg market. The only individual who was taking up options was Mr. John I. McFarland. As to how low wheat would have have gone if this action had not been taken, I do not know, but the fact is that there were days when you could not sell Canadian wheat on the Winnipeg market. While I should like to say that the government should not divulge this information, as I said before, I do not see where any good could come out of giving it and there might possibly be some harm.
